title: Blondie (band)
wiki_lead:
Blondie is an American rock band formed in New York City in 1974 by singer Debbie Harry and guitarist Chris Stein. Emerging as a pioneer of the early new wave genre from the CBGB punk scene of the mid-1970s, the band subsequently achieved global commercial success with their third studio album, Parallel Lines (1978). The record launched a string of international hit singles, including "Heart of Glass", "Call Me", and "Rapture". Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2006, the group has sold over 40 million records worldwide.
While Blondie's self-titled debut album, Blondie (1976), remained a strictly underground release, their second album, Plastic Letters (1978), brought the band their first commercial success in the United Kingdom and Australia. However, they remained largely unknown to mainstream audiences in their native United States until the release of their third studio album, Parallel Lines (1978). The record became an international breakthrough, selling an estimated 20 million copies worldwide. Over the next three years, the band achieved global chart dominance, releasing a string of hit singles through their follow-up albums Eat to the Beat (1979) and Autoamerican (1980). Their most successful tracks from this era included "Heart of Glass" (U.S. and U.K. No. 1), "One Way or Another", "Dreaming", "Call Me" (from the American Gigolo soundtrack; U.S. and U.K. No. 1), "Atomic", "The Tide Is High" (U.S. and U.K. No. 1), and "Rapture" (U.S. No. 1), which became the first "Billboard" number-one singles to feature rap vocals.
Blondie disbanded in late 1982 following the commercial failure of their sixth studio album, The Hunter (1982), which was compounded by internal tensions, financial difficulties, and the severe illness of co-founder and guitarist Chris Stein. Harry subsequently paused her career to care for Stein, who was diagnosed with pemphigus, a rare and life-threatening autoimmune disease of the skin. The band re-formed in 1997, achieving renewed success with their seventh album No Exit (1999) and their sixth number one single in the U.K. with "Maria" in 1999, exactly 20 years after their first U.K. number one single, "Heart of Glass".
The group toured and performed throughout the world during the following years, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2006. Blondie has sold over 40 million records worldwide and continues to actively perform. The band's eleventh studio album, Pollinator, was released on May 5, 2017, charting at number 4 in the U.K. A new studio album, High Noon, has been announced for release on February 26, 2027.

Emerging as a pioneer of the early new wave genre from the CBGB punk scene of the mid-1970s, the band subsequently achieved global commercial success with their third studio album, Parallel Lines (1978). However, they remained largely unknown to mainstream audiences in their native United States until the release of their third studio album, Parallel Lines (1978). The record became an international breakthrough, selling an estimated 20 million copies worldwide. Over the next three years, the band achieved global chart dominance, releasing a string of hit singles through their follow-up albums Eat to the Beat (1979) and Autoamerican (1980). Their most successful tracks from this era included "Heart of Glass" (U.S. and U.K. No. 1), "One Way or Another", "Dreaming", "Call Me" (from the American Gigolo soundtrack; U.S. and U.K. No. 1), "Atomic", "The Tide Is High" (U.S. and U.K. No. 1), and "Rapture" (U.S. No. 1), which became the first "Billboard" number-one singles to feature rap vocals.
Blondie disbanded in late 1982 following the commercial failure of their sixth studio album, The Hunter (1982), which was compounded by internal tensions, financial difficulties, and the severe illness of co-founder and guitarist Chris Stein. Harry subsequently paused her career to care for Stein, who was diagnosed with pemphigus, a rare and life-threatening autoimmune disease of the skin. The band re-formed in 1997, achieving renewed success with their seventh album No Exit (1999) and their sixth number one single in the U.K. with "Maria" in 1999, exactly 20 years after their first U.K. number one single, "Heart of Glass".
The group toured and performed throughout the world during the following years, and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2006. Blondie has sold over 40 million records worldwide and continues to actively perform. The band's eleventh studio album, Pollinator, was released on May 5, 2017, charting at number 4 in the U.K. A new studio album, High Noon, has been announced for release on February 26, 2027.


History


1974–1978: Early career
Inspired by the burgeoning new music scene at the Mercer Arts Center in Manhattan, musician Chris Stein sought a band with similar interests. He joined the Stilettoes in 1973 as their guitarist and formed a romantic relationship with Debbie Harry, who was one of the band's vocalists, a former waitress and Playboy Bunny. Harry had previously been a member of the late-1960s folk-rock group The Wind in the Willows. In July 1974, Stein and Harry left the Stilettoes and formed a new ensemble with ex-Stilettoes bandmates Billy O'Connor on drums (born 1953, died 2015) and Fred Smith on bass.
Originally billed as Angel and the Snake for two performances in August 1974, the group renamed themselves Blondie and the Banzai Babies, shortening it to Blondie by October 1974. Guitarist Ivan Kral subsequently joined the lineup, alongside vocalists Tish and Snooky Bellomo, who contributed occasional live backing vocals for over a year and a half. The chosen name was derived from catcalls truck drivers frequently directed at Harry while she walked down Houston Street after bleaching her hair blonde.
By early 1975, O'Connor had left the music industry, and Fred Smith replaced Richard Hell in Television, while Ivan Kral eventually joined the Patti Smith Group. Stein and Harry continued the ensemble, embarking on auditions that recruited longtime drummer Clem Burke and bassist Gary Valentine. Within weeks of this reorganization, the Bellomo sisters were let go from the group without notice.
Blondie became regular performers at Max's Kansas City and CBGB. In June 1975, the band recorded their inaugural demo, produced by Alan Betrock. To fill out their instrumentation, they recruited keyboardist Jimmy Destri in November 1975. The band eventually signed with Private Stock Records, releasing their debut single, "X-Offender", in June 1976, followed by their self-titled debut studio album, Blondie, in December 1976. Neither release achieved initial commercial success, and the band spent the remainder of the year touring as a supporting act for Television and embarking on their first promotional trip to the U.K.
In early 1977, Blondie was invited to open for David Bowie and Iggy Pop on the U.S. leg of the Idiot World Tour supporting Pop's debut solo album, The Idiot, after the pair heard and admired Blondie's debut record. In July 1977, Gary Valentine left the band to pursue solo ventures and form his own group, the Know; he was replaced on bass by Frank Infante.
In September 1977, the band bought out their contract with Private Stock and signed with the British label Chrysalis Records. The debut album was subsequently re-released on the new label in October 1977. Rolling Stone's review of the record observed the eclectic nature of the group's music, comparing its style to both Phil Spector and the Who, while noting that the album's primary strengths were Richard Gottehrer's production and the distinct persona of Harry.

The band's first major commercial breakthrough occurred in Australia later that year, when the music television program Countdown mistakenly played the music video for "In the Flesh"—the B-side to their debut single "X-Offender". Jimmy Destri later credited the show's host, Molly Meldrum, for the band's initial Australian success, remarking that "we still thank him to this day" for broadcasting the wrong track. In a 1998 retrospective, Burke recalled watching the broadcast of the episode, though both he and Chris Stein suggested that the song choice may have been a deliberate subterfuge by Meldrum. Stein asserted that "X-Offender" was "too crazy and aggressive" to become a mainstream hit, whereas "In the Flesh" was "not representative of any punk sensibility. Over the years, I've thought they probably played both things but liked one better. That's all." Burke subsequently described "In the Flesh" as an early "forerunner to the power ballad".
The single subsequently reached number two in Australia, and the album entered the Australian top twenty in November 1977. A subsequent double-A-side reissue of "X-Offender" and "Rip Her to Shreds" peaked at number 81 on the national chart. A successful Australian concert tour followed in December 1977, though it was marred by an incident on December 8 at Her Majesty's Theatre in Brisbane, where disappointed fans nearly rioted after Harry cancelled the performance due to illness; the concert was later rescheduled and performed on December 18.
In February 1978, Blondie released their second studio album, Plastic Letters (U.K. number 10, U.S. number 78, Australia number 64). The album was recorded in mid-1977, with the group officially operating as a quartet following Gary Valentine's departure on July 4, 1977. Frank Infante was brought in as a session musician to play bass on the sessions and is credited on all issues of the record with bass and rhythm guitar; Stein is credited with lead guitar, bass, E-bow, and vibes. Plastic Letters was promoted extensively throughout Europe and Asia by Chrysalis Records.
The album's lead single, "Denis", was a cover version of Randy and the Rainbows' 1963 hit "Denise". It reached number two on the U.K. Singles Chart, while both the album and its second single, "(I'm Always Touched by Your) Presence, Dear" (written by Valentine), reached the British top ten. This chart success, along with a highly successful U.K. tour that included a landmark performance at London's Roundhouse on March 5, 1978, made Blondie one of the first American new wave bands to achieve mainstream commercial crossover in the U.K. After the album's release, Infante was integrated as an official band member and switched to guitar, while British musician Nigel Harrison was hired as the group's full-time bassist. This expanded Blondie into a six-piece for the first time, marking a long-term stabilization in the band's lineup.


1978–1981: Mainstream success

Blondie completed the recording of their third studio album, Parallel Lines, in mid-1978 with Australian producer Mike Chapman. Released in September of that year, the record reached number one in the U.K, number six in the US, and number two in Australia. It finally broke the band into the mainstream American market on the strength of the worldwide hit single "Heart of Glass". Parallel Lines became the group's most commercially successful album, eventually selling 20 million copies worldwide. The album's first two European singles were "Picture This" (U.K. number 12) and "Hanging on the Telephone" (U.K. number five). Because the band had previously found success with a cover track, Chrysalis Records selected their version of Buddy Holly's "I'm Gonna Love You Too" as the lead single from Parallel Lines in the US. This strategy proved to be a miscalculation, as the single failed to chart.
"Heart of Glass" was released as a single in early 1979. The disco-infused track topped the U.K. Singles Chart in February 1979, and reached number one on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100 in April 1979. The song was a complete reworking of a rock and reggae-influenced track originally titled "Once I Had a Love" (or "The Disco Song"), which the group had performed since its formation in the mid-1970s before updating it with prominent elements of disco music. Burke later noted that the revamped arrangement was inspired partly by Kraftwerk and partly by the Bee Gees' "Stayin' Alive", whose driving drum beat Burke attempted to emulate. Both he and Stein gave Destri substantial credit for the final composition, remarking that Destri's appreciation for emerging studio technology had prompted him to introduce synthesizers and completely reformat the keyboard layers.
Although some contemporary music critics condemned Blondie for "selling out" by incorporating dance-pop aesthetics, the single became a massive international success and one of the highest-selling records of 1979. As the visual and stylistic focal point of the group, Harry began to attain a level of mainstream celebrity status that increasingly set her apart from her bandmates. During this period, she also embarked on an acting career, appearing in the independent feature film The Foreigner (1978), directed by Amos Poe.
Blondie's follow-up single in the U.S. was the more aggressive rock song "One Way or Another" (U.S. number 24), while in the U.K, an alternate single selection, "Sunday Girl", became a number-one hit. Parallel Lines has since been ranked at number 140 on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time. A major cover feature on the band photographed by Annie Leibovitz subsequently appeared in Rolling Stone magazine in June 1979. The group returned to the studio with producer Mike Chapman to begin tracking their follow-up album in the summer of 1979.
Blondie's fourth studio album, Eat to the Beat (U.K. number one, U.S. number seventeen, Australia number nine), also produced by Chapman, was released in September 1979. Although well received by critics as a suitable follow-up to Parallel Lines, the album and its accompanying singles failed to achieve the same level of commercial success in the US. In the UK, the album delivered three top 20 hits, including the band's third UK number-one single, "Atomic" (U.S. number thirty-nine). grok_lead: Blondie is an American rock band formed in New York City in 1974 by vocalist Debbie Harry and guitarist Chris Stein, emerging as pioneers of the new wave genre through their fusion of punk, pop, disco, and hip-hop elements. The band rose to global prominence in the late 1970s with multi-platinum albums like Parallel Lines (1978), which sold over 20 million copies worldwide, and chart-topping singles including "Heart of Glass," "Call Me," "The Tide Is High," and "Rapture," amassing four number-one hits on the Billboard Hot 100. After disbanding in 1982 amid internal tensions, Blondie reunited in 1997, achieving further success with the UK number-one single "Maria" from No Exit (1999) and continued releases such as Pollinator (2017), while selling more than 40 million records overall. Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2006, the group remains active as of 2025, with a new studio album, High Noon, slated for release in spring 2026 featuring production by John Congleton and final recordings from late drummer Clem Burke, who passed away in April 2025. The band's original lineup included drummer Clem Burke, keyboardist Jimmy Destri, and bassist Gary Valentine, with early performances at iconic venues like CBGB shaping their raw, energetic sound amid New York's punk scene. Following their breakthrough, Blondie experimented across genresâincorporating reggae in "The Tide Is High," rap in "Rapture" (the first with a rapper to top the US charts), and electronic elementsâbefore their initial split due to exhaustion and personal challenges. The 1997 reunion revitalized their career, leading to six UK number-one singles in total, including "Atomic" and "Sunday Girl," and albums that blended nostalgia with modern production. As of 2025, Blondie's core creative force consists of Debbie Harry and Chris Stein, with Stein contributing primarily in the studio; the touring and recording lineup features bassist Leigh Foxx, keyboardist Matt Katz-Bohen, and guitarist Tommy Kessler. Their influence extends to fashion, MTV-era visuals, and gender dynamics in rock, with Harry's iconic image and versatile songwriting defining an era of boundary-pushing pop stardom. Despite lineup changes and the recent loss of Burke, Blondie persists as a enduring act, preparing what may be their final album while maintaining a legacy of innovation and commercial triumph.
